newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban say ex-Afghan president Najibullah executed.
newsitem.headline: Taleban say ex-Afghan president Najibullah executed.

text.p: Taleban commanders said on Friday they had hanged former Afghan president Najibullah and his brother Shahpur Ahmadzai after the capture of Kabul.
The bodies of the two men were hanging from a concrete traffic-control post at the gates of the presidential palace as a crowd of more than a thousand people crowded around to watch.
I saw Najibullah's body, battered and bloody, hanging with a steel wire noose around the neck.
"We killed him because he was the murderer of our people," Noor Hakmal, a Taleban commander who entered the city from Charasyab, south of Kabul overnight, told Reuters.
Hakmal said the Taleban was searching the city for President Burhanuddin Rabbani, Prime Minister Gulbuddin Hekmatyar and military chief Ahmad Shah Masood but there was no word on their whereabouts.
The burly Najibullah had lived in the United Nations office in Kabul since April 1992 when he was ousted by mujahideen guerrilla forces after 14 years of civil war.
Ahmadzai was a former security chief under Najibullah's Soviet-backed government.
Earlier Taleban leaders said they had taken control of Kabul and met with no resistance from government forces.

They vowed to enforce an Islamic system in the country. A statement by Mullah Omar, quoted by the Afghan Islamic Press news agency in Pakistan, delared Afghanistan a "completely Islamic state" where a "complete Islamic system will be enforced".

Celebratory bursts of machine-gun fire and occasional explosions echoed across the city at dawn but the Afghan capital was relatively calm as Taleban fighters set up checkpoints to search vehicles, the witnesses said.
All key government installations appeared to be in Taleban hands including the Presidential Palace and the Ministries of Defence, Security and Foreign Affairs.
No government forces were visible on the city's streets.
Troops had been seen leaving Kabul some hours before, on the only government-controlled road out of Kabul.
Witnesses said a convoy of four-wheeled drive vehicles and cars left the city during the night and government forces blew up several ammunition dumps before they retreated.
Taleban commandsers said they had also captured Bagram airbase, 50 km (30 miles) north of Kabul, as well as the disused Kabul airport near the city.
Witnesses said tanks, artillery and trucks loaded with soldiers headed north, apparently towards Jabal us-Sharaj, the headquarters of military chief Masood at the entrance to the Panjshir valley.
Kabul itself was quiet on Friday. Civilians were walking in the streets in the morning past Taleban fighters manning checkpoints and crossroads.
Some people were returning to their homes in the eastern suburbs laden with belongings after fleeing earlier fighting.
